blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant sugar beet. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

Sugar beet is rarely grown in the Philippines: there is no beet sugar mill here, and only trial plots of tropical sugar beet types have been planted. This short guide shows how those few growers handle it, sown in the cool dry months and dug about five months later.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for root crops](/land-preparation/root-crop-land-preparation).
When to plant sugar beet

Tropical sugar beet does best when sown at the start of the cool dry months, around November, in the lowlands or mid elevations, so the roots fill before the hot months. Late sowing gives smaller roots and less sugar.
What you plant
Seed of tropical sugar beet types, sown straight in the field, usually two seeds a hill, thinned later to one plant.
Paano magtanim ng sugar beet, step by step
The crop is ready about 160 days after sowing.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 14 days before sowing: Plow deep and fertilize
items.text: Plow and harrow until the soil is deep and fine. Work in the phosphorus, potash and boron with about a third of the nitrogen during the last harrowing.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Sowing day: Sow in rows
items.text: Sow two seeds a hill in rows about 50 cm apart with hills about 20 cm apart, and water if the soil is dry.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 20: First weeding
items.text: Hand weed the rows while the seedlings are small. Young beets cannot compete with weeds.

items.title: Day 40: Second weeding and thinning
items.text: Weed again and pull the weaker seedling so one plant stays in each hill.

items.title: Day 60: Top dress and earth up
items.text: Give half of the remaining urea, weed for the last time and pull soil up around the roots.

items.title: Day 70: Check for root rot
items.text: Look for wilting plants with rotting crowns or white fungus at the base, and pull them out.

items.title: Day 100: Last top dressing and earthing up
items.text: Give the rest of the urea and earth up again. Water in long dry spells.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Day 160: Dig the roots
items.text: Roots are richest in sugar at about 150 to 165 days after the seedlings come up. Dig them out, cut off the tops and deliver them quickly, since sugar drops after digging.

blocks.text: Watering sugar beet, stage by stage

Sugar beet is very rarely grown in the Philippines, only in trials. It is sown into moist soil at the start of the cool dry months, around November, and watered by furrow in long dry spells, with the rows kept draining because standing water rots the roots. Furrow irrigation between the rows, in the morning or late afternoon.

blocks.title: Never let sugar beet go dry at these stages
blocks.text: Sowing to a full stand. Leaf growth and root filling, when the plant builds its size.

blocks.caption: Watering schedule for sugar beet, stage by stage
rows: Sow into moist soil after the rains. Water the furrows if the soil is dry
A light furrow watering that wets the rows without crusting them
Furrow water in dry spells. Water before thinning and after top dressing
Keep watering by furrow in long dry spells. Water in the last top dressing
Soak the rows, never standing water
Stop watering about three to four weeks before digging, but keep some moisture so the roots do not break
No water, or one light watering if the soil turns hard

blocks.text:
**Without irrigation.** Sow at the start of the cool dry months, around November, so the crop starts on the moisture left after the rains. Late sowing gives smaller roots and less sugar.

**In the dry season.** Water by furrow in long dry spells through leaf growth and root filling, and stop about three to four weeks before digging. Water when the leaves stay limp into the late afternoon.

**In the rainy season.** Plant on ridges with open furrows and avoid fields that flood. Standing water rots the roots.

items: **Too little water:** Leaves wilt through the afternoon, the canopy stays thin, and the roots stay small.
**Too much water:** Leaves yellow and the roots rot from the tip or crown.

blocks.text: To water better for a higher yield: Water steadily through leaf growth and stop three to four weeks before digging for more sugar. Watering every other furrow saves water with little loss of yield.
Spacing, water and fertilizer for sugar beet
Spacing
Rows about 50 cm apart and hills about 20 cm apart, thinned to one plant a hill.
Water
Sown into moist soil after the rains and watered by furrow in long dry spells. Standing water rots the roots.
Fertilizer

Trial plots use balanced fertilizer by soil test, with about a third of the nitrogen at land preparation and the rest as urea in two top dressings at about 60 and 100 days. Beets need boron. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-plants).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows
Hand weeding at about 20, 40 and 60 days, thinning to one plant a hill at the second weeding, and earthing up at the top dressings.
When and how to harvest
Dug about five to five and a half months after the seedlings come up, topped and sent to the buyer the same day or the next.
Common mistakes when planting sugar beet

items: Planting without a buyer or mill nearby to take the roots.
Sowing late in the cool season, which cuts root size and sugar.
Skipping thinning, so roots stay small.
Planting on poorly drained land, where root rot spreads.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of sugar beet
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Plant only under contract or a trial program with a sure buyer.
Use tropical sugar beet seed, not temperate types.
Test the soil and include boron.
Sow on time at the start of the cool dry months and harvest on time.

blocks.text: Questions about planting sugar beet

items.a: Sugar beet is rarely grown in the Philippines: there is no beet sugar mill here, and only trial plots of tropical sugar beet types have been planted. Follow the steps above in order, from getting the field ready to the harvest, then change one thing at a time for a higher yield.

items.q: When do farmers plant sugar beet in the Philippines?
items.a: Tropical sugar beet does best when sown at the start of the cool dry months, around November, in the lowlands or mid elevations, so the roots fill before the hot months. Late sowing gives smaller roots and less sugar.

items.q: How far apart do you plant sugar beet?
items.a: Rows about 50 cm apart and hills about 20 cm apart, thinned to one plant a hill.

items.q: How long before sugar beet can be harvested?
items.a: It is ready about 160 days after sowing. Dug about five to five and a half months after the seedlings come up, topped and sent to the buyer the same day or the next.

items.q: How often do you water sugar beet?
items.a: Sowing to coming up, sowing day to day 14: Sow into moist soil after the rains. Water the furrows if the soil is dry. Leaf growth, day 14 to 60: Furrow water in dry spells. Water before thinning and after top dressing. Roots filling, day 60 to 130: Keep watering by furrow in long dry spells. Water in the last top dressing. Water by furrow in long dry spells through leaf growth and root filling, and stop about three to four weeks before digging.

items.q: What do you plant to grow sugar beet?
items.a: Seed of tropical sugar beet types, sown straight in the field, usually two seeds a hill, thinned later to one plant.
